stances.claim: Courts must engage new sciences because giant strides in science and technology change human behavior and social interaction and require new modes of governance and new jurisprudential norms without precedence.

stances.claim: Reproductive cloning via somatic cell nuclear transfer challenges the Civil Code's Article 40 'conceived child' framework — because the cloned child is not the result of normal fertilization of egg by sperm, and Article 40's personality-by-birth rule presupposes conception in the traditional sense.
stances.evidence: Civil Code Article 40 text; cloning procedure mechanics

stances.claim: Maternity and paternity become contested categories under cloning: is the mother Marie (cell origin) or Katrina (gestational/birth)? Is the father Pedro? Juan? — forcing courts to develop categorical refinements (legal, biological, surrogate, adoptive parents).
stances.evidence: Specific facts of the fictional case; Family Code filiation rules

stances.claim: Family Code filiation rules do not cleanly fit cloning: filiation is by nature or adoption; legitimacy presupposes conception or birth during marriage; artificial insemination requires written-instrument ratification before birth — none of which match the cloning fact-pattern.
stances.evidence: Family Code text laid out against fictional facts

stances.claim: Without offering definitive answers, the author argues that surfacing the questions themselves vindicates judicial engagement with new sciences — and points the curious to his 2003 book for further exploration.
stances.rhetorical_move: questions-as-vindication move; deferral to author's prior work

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why the Supreme Court and he have been interested in the latest in science and technology, harkening back to his 2003 book 'The Bio-age Dawns on the Judiciary' and to the SC's early DNA cases Tijing v. Court of Appeals (March 8, 2001) and People v. Vallejo (May 9, 2002): giant strides in science change human behavior and social interaction and require new modes of governance and new jurisprudential norms without precedence -- as they still do today. To illustrate, he sums up a fictional thought-experiment from his book: in 1998, Pedro (a Filipino) and Marie (an Italian) marry; their obstetrician diagnoses Marie as incapable of conceiving, causing frustration and separation; from the internet, Marie learns about somatic cell nuclear transfer (reproductive cloning) -- a cell nucleus is extracted from a donor's tissue (skin or mammary), inserted into an egg cell whose nucleus has been removed, chemically and electronically stimulated to divide, and implanted into a human uterus; over Pedro's vehement objection, Marie travels to a Hong Kong fertility clinic with her best friend Katrina (British, married to the Filipino physician Dr. Juan); in Hong Kong, a nucleus from Marie's skin is inserted into a denucleated egg, the resulting zygote divides, and over Dr. Juan's vehement objection it is transferred to Katrina's womb as surrogate mother; the cloned baby Carmina is born; Marie and Katrina return to the Philippines with Carmina and reside together separately from their Filipino husbands. The cascading legal questions are: Is Carmina a 'person' in legal contemplation, or merely an 'extension' of a human cell and tissue? Civil Code Article 40 says 'birth determines personality' -- but the determination refers to a 'conceived child,' so does it apply to one not conceived (not the result of normal fertilization of egg by sperm)? Is she entitled to be accorded 'birth' and 'personality' qualities 'favorable to it' under Article 41? When was she conceived? How was her intrauterine life determined? Who is her mother -- Marie (whose cell she originated from) or Katrina (whose womb carried, nurtured, and birthed her)? Who is her father -- Pedro? Juan? Is she legitimate or illegitimate? How is filiation established? Will a DNA test sustain her identity and parentage? If she is merely an extension of an original person, is she actually Marie's sister, and therefore the daughter of Marie's parents whose chromosomes she shares? Are we prepared to classify parents as legal, biological, surrogate, or adoptive? Family Code provides that filiation may be by nature or adoption; that children conceived or born during the marriage are legitimate; that artificial-insemination children may be legitimate if both spouses authorized or ratified the procedure in a written instrument executed before birth; and that children conceived or born outside valid marriages are illegitimate. In the fictional case, cloning is hardly natural; it is not artificial insemination (no sperm involved); no written instrument was executed -- so was Carmina conceived or born within or outside the valid existing marriages of Pedro-Marie and Juan-Katrina? Many more questions, including ethical and moral, remain -- for lack of space, the author ends, confident that the basic question of why courts are interested in new sciences has been answered, and points the curious to his 2003 book.
